## Solution

We work over a non-perfect field $k$. A convenient choice throughout is $k = \mathbb{F}_p(t)$, the rational function field in one variable over $\mathbb{F}_p$ (where $p$ is a prime). Recall that $k$ is not perfect: the element $t \in k$ has no $p$-th root in $k$, since $t \notin k^p = \mathbb{F}_p(t^p)$.

For each part we produce an affine $k$-scheme $X = \operatorname{Spec} A$ and verify the required properties by examining the base change $X_{\bar{k}} = \operatorname{Spec}(A \otimes_k \bar{k})$, where $\bar{k}$ is an algebraic closure.

---

### (a) Reduced but not geometrically reduced

Take
$$A = k[x]/(x^p - t), \qquad X = \operatorname{Spec} A.$$

**$X$ is reduced.** The polynomial $f(x) = x^p - t$ is irreducible over $k$: if it factored, it would have a root in $k$, i.e. some $u \in k$ with $u^p = t$; but $t \notin k^p$, contradiction. (Equivalently, $x^p - t$ is the minimal polynomial of $t^{1/p}$ over $k$, since $[k(t^{1/p}):k] = p$.) Being irreducible, $(x^p - t)$ is prime, so $A$ is an integral domain, hence reduced.

**$X$ is not geometrically reduced.** Over $\bar{k}$ we may pick $\alpha \in \bar{k}$ with $\alpha^p = t$. Then in $\bar{k}[x]$,
$$x^p - t = x^p - \alpha^p = (x - \alpha)^p,$$
so
$$A \otimes_k \bar{k} \;\cong\; \bar{k}[x]/(x-\alpha)^p.$$
This ring has nilpotents (the class of $x - \alpha$ is nonzero and nilpotent of index $p$), so it is **not** reduced. Therefore $X_{\bar{k}}$ is not reduced, i.e. $X$ is not geometrically reduced.

---

### (b) Connected but not geometrically connected

Take
$$A = k[x]/(x^p - t), \qquad X = \operatorname{Spec} A,$$
the **same** scheme as in part (a).

**$X$ is connected.** As shown above, $A$ is an integral domain, hence $X = \operatorname{Spec} A$ is irreducible (in particular connected).

**$X$ is not geometrically connected.** Over $\bar{k}$, with $\alpha^p = t$,
$$A \otimes_k \bar{k} \;\cong\; \bar{k}[x]/(x-\alpha)^p.$$
This local artinian ring has a single prime ideal $(x-\alpha)$, so $\operatorname{Spec}$ of it is a single point — wait, that *is* connected. Let me use a cleaner separable example instead.

Take $k = \mathbb{R}$ and
$$A = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2 + 1), \qquad X = \operatorname{Spec} A.$$

**$X$ is connected.** The polynomial $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$, so $A \cong \mathbb{C}$ is a field. Thus $X = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C}$ is a single point, hence connected (even irreducible).

**$X$ is not geometrically connected.** Over $\bar{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{C}$,
$$x^2 + 1 = (x - i)(x + i),$$
so
$$A \otimes_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{C} \;\cong\; \mathbb{C}[x]/(x-i)(x+i) \;\cong\; \mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}.$$
By the Chinese remainder theorem (the ideals $(x-i)$ and $(x+i)$ are comaximal in $\mathbb{C}[x]$). Therefore
$$X_{\mathbb{C}} = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C} \;\sqcup\; \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{C},$$
a disjoint union of **two** points, which is **disconnected**. Hence $X$ is not geometrically connected.

---

### (c) Integral but not geometrically integral

Take
$$A = k[x]/(x^p - t), \qquad X = \operatorname{Spec} A, \qquad k = \mathbb{F}_p(t),$$
the same scheme as in part (a).

**$X$ is integral.** As established, $A$ is an integral domain, so $X$ is both reduced and irreducible, hence integral.

**$X$ is not geometrically integral.** Over $\bar{k}$,
$$A \otimes_k \bar{k} \;\cong\; \bar{k}[x]/(x - \alpha)^p,$$
which has nilpotents (so it is not reduced) and in particular is not an integral domain. Therefore $X_{\bar{k}}$ is not integral, i.e. $X$ is not geometrically integral.

In fact $X_{\bar{k}}$ fails *both* conditions for integrality: it is non-reduced (hence not geometrically reduced, consistent with (a)) and, while its underlying topological space is a single point (so it is "geometrically connected" in the topological sense), the scheme is not geometrically *irreducible* as a scheme because the local ring is non-reduced — a scheme is geometrically integral iff it remains both reduced and irreducible after base change, and here reducedness fails.

---

### Summary table

| Part | $k$ | Scheme | Satisfies | Fails after $\otimes_k \bar{k}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ | $\operatorname{Spec} k[x]/(x^p - t)$ | reduced | reduced (becomes $(x-\alpha)^p$, nilpotents) |
| (b) | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)$ | connected | connected (splits into $\mathbb{C}\sqcup\mathbb{C}$) |
| (c) | $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ | $\operatorname{Spec} k[x]/(x^p - t)$ | integral | integral (non-reduced, so non-integral) |

The unifying mechanism: a non-perfect (resp. non-algebraically-closed) field $k$ admits irreducible polynomials that become **non-square-free** (purely inseparable, part (a)/(c)) or **reducible** (separable splitting, part (b)) over $\bar{k}$, so the corresponding affine scheme — integral/connected over $k$ — degenerates after geometric base change.

### PROOF COMPLETE
